children.name: viewing pattern
children.full: Tell me about your pattern of watching movies
children.script:
Ok, I'm gonna tell you about my patterns of watching movies.

As you know, I am really busy all the time so I have no choice but to watch movies on weekends. Unfortunately, the weekend is not solely my time because I have my two sons to take care of. In this sense, watching movies is one of the best ways to spend time with them.

Our favorite theater is the multiplex "World tower" which is just a ten-minute walk away. As the theater is located in the Lotte-world tower complex, there are lots of things to enjoy before and after watching movies.

I have my routines to do before watching movies, so let me share it with you. Visiting popular trendy pop-ups is an essential course before watching movies.  First, we need to scramble to add our slot to the waiting list and then head over to the Lexus cafe to wait for our turn. Well, don't be embarrassed even though you get the waiting number two thousand! It only takes time to have a cup of coffee. Oh, visiting the concession stand before getting into the auditorium is essential.

After the movie, we usually starve to have lunch. My appetite is Italians, but my young boys have no choice but to have Korean meals. We often visit "House of Korean", where the kids menu is well served at a reasonable price.

These are all about my pattern of watching movies and the activities before and after watching movies. I really wish I could fully enjoy a movie all on my own. Well, I imagine my future watching the movie "pororo and friends" this weekend.

children.name: movies then vs. now
children.full: Compare the movies today to those that you saw while you were growing up. Discuss how movies have changed. Tell me about the similarities and differences between them
children.script:
You know, I often watch old movies with my little two sons, so I'm realizing the changes of movies over time. Let me tell you about it.

Recently, my sons and I are watching a movie called "Frog and Toad" made in 1985. The movie was made by stop-motion animation, so-called clay animation, and I was deeply impressed to know how to make the movie. Can you believe that every scene is created using real clay figures or dolls, with 5 frames captured every second? I cannot imagine how labor-intensive it is! The labor did not end even in the era of Walt Disney, 1940's. Directors should draw thousands of hand-drawn pictures to make a single movie. But you know, nowadays, making computer graphics is a super-easy task with the aid of AI technology.

The method of watching movies also has been changed. When I was young, there is no way but to go to video rentals to watch movies at home. That was a point that the founder of Netflix though uncomfortable. Nowadays, OTT is very popular and I am also subscribing to a few platforms such as Netflix, amazon prime, apple tv and so on. However, it's a pity that we cannot pick out tapes at a video rental anymore, leaving it to our memory.

Oh, I said only the differences of the movies. You know, I feel like I'm having a time-travel with my sons. I feel like I'm going back to my youth when I'm looking at my sons happily watching Frog and Toad or pocket monster animations, which were my favorites. It is the most similar thing between the old movies and recent movies that they both bring happiness to my family.

Open the door, put the dishes and detergents into the dishwasher, and press the start button! It really reduces the time to finish the dishwashing, liberating me from this tedious labor.

Another house chore on me is laundry. Our family is four, so a tremendous amount of laundry comes out every day. Just put a bunch of clothes to the machine, and put detergent and fabric softeners, and finally press the start button! It's easy huh?

children.name: housing problems
children.full: What are some major problems people have when they rent a home or an apartment? How do people deal with these issues? How do these things affect how or where people live?
children.script: The biggest problem that people face is probably regarding rent prices, especially if you work and live in a big city like Seoul. Although there are many apartments and houses, people complain that they don't have a place to live because of the hiking prices. Simply put, over 10% of the entire population live in Seoul and there aren't enough houses to fit all of them. To make matters worse, bank interest is soaring these days because of Iran War. So tenants tend to choose to live on the outskirts of Seoul because they can no longer afford the high mortgage interest. To solve this problem, the government is constructing more and more satellite cities outside of Seoul, hoping it would scatter the population but it hasn't been so successful so far. The government also tries to replace the Yongsan Family Park with apartments to provide houses in Seoul, but many people are against the policy right now in that it may violate Seoul citizen's right to health. Honestly, I don't really know how we can solve this sort of problem. The government failed to stabilize the rent prices every now and then, so many people have no expectations any more. Building more houses is the only way to lower rental prices, well, they don't just pop out of an oven like bread ! Yeah, it's a really difficult problem to solve.

Oh Eva, that's an interesting question. Well, these days young people in Korea are crazy about big tech companies — Samsung and SK Hynix in semiconductors, and IT companies like Naver or Kakao. And in my opinion, it all narrows down to two things: the culture and the benefits.

First of all, they want a company where they can grow together with the company itself. Nobody wants to be just another cog in the machine — they want a place where they can spread their wings and make their dreams come true. And what really matters to them is a horizontal atmosphere, where even a rookie's opinion is respected instead of being ignored just because of age or position. Not to mention, they put a lot of emphasis on work-life balance. They want to take a vacation without feeling self-conscious about their boss, and they prefer flexible working hours so they can design their own schedule.

On top of that, benefits and location make a huge difference. Actually, there's a funny expression here in Korea — the "southern limit line." It originally comes from the DMZ, but young job seekers use it to mean the psychological line they refuse to go below. For engineers, that line is Pyeongtaek, so if a company is located any further south, they simply don't apply, no matter how good the offer is. And the small things count too — a nice cafeteria with free meals, a shuttle bus running from Seoul, and a generous allowance for team dinners.

So all in all, young people today are looking for much more than just a high salary. That's it, Eva!

children.name: internet security & addiction
children.full: What are some issues people talk about regarding the internet? What are their concerns and why are those concerns a problem? Are security problems on the internet a problem? If so, talk about that issue.
children.script:
Oh Eva, that's a serious topic. As people spend more and more time online, two issues keep coming up. It's a security problem, and internet addiction. There are some good examples that occurred recently this year.

Regarding the security problem, actually, it happened to me. Not long ago, one of the biggest shopping platforms in Korea, Coupang, had a massive data leak. Someone stole the personal information of over thirty million users, including names, phone numbers, and home addresses. And my account was one of them. Ever since then, I keep getting calls from voice fishing scammers, and it makes me shudder every time when an unknown number pops up on my screen. You know, I've heard that the latest frontier AI models, the ones from OpenAI or Anthropic, are getting incredibly good at hacking. So I'm pretty sure security problems will get bigger and bigger from now on.

The other issue is addiction, and there was huge news about it just a few days ago. Meta agreed to pay around billions of dollars to settle a lawsuit that said Instragram was intentionally made to get teens addicted. This tells you how serious the problem is. Many kids these days can't concentrate on their studies at all, they just scroll through Reels all day long. Meta promised to set a daily limit of two hours for teens. I really hope it works out.

So all in all, the internet is a double-edged sword, and it's our responsibility to use it wisely. That's it, Eva!

children.name: internet across generations
children.full: How is internet usage different among generations? What do younger people commonly do online, and what do older people do online?
children.script:
Oh Eva, that's an interesting question, and yes, there's a huge gap between generations. Simply put, older people use the internet in a pretty limited way while younger people do almost everything online.

Well, it's already been over three decades since the internet first launched. Since then, the government has provided a lot of free education programs for senior citizens, so these days even older people are comfortable with simple web searching and watching YouTube. My parents are a perfect example. Honestly, they watch YouTube all day long. Well, it's a bit worrying, to be honest.

Young people, in contrast, don't stop at YouTube. They're crazy about short-form content like Reels, they trade stocks online, they order food delivery, and you name it. And with AI booming these days, they're trying all kinds of new things like creating funny images, or even producing short films. Actually, I'm one of them. I'm totally hooked on so-called "vibe coding" these days. I built my own app using Claude, an app that really helps me with my studies, and I'm more than satisfied with it.

So all in all, the older generation mainly consumes what the internet gives them, while the younger generation actually creates something with it. That's the biggest difference, Eva!

children.name: weather in your country
children.full: Tell me about the weather conditions in your country.
children.script:
Oh Eva, that's an interesting question. Korea actually has four distinct seasons – spring, summer, fall and winter. But these days, due to global warming, summers are getting hotter and winters are getting colder, so spring and fall have almost disappeared in recent years. even there anymore. As a spring-lover, it's too sad, but let me focus on summer and winter, since those are the two seasons that really define my country.

Let's begin with summer. It often rains a lot in summer, but due to global warming, we're seeing more tropical-like downpours lately. These torrential rains often hit specific, localized areas and sadly, result in people getting injured. On clear days, it is usually hot and humid so many people head to the beach to cool down from the scorching heat. Beyond just water sports and sunbathing, Korea is also widely known for its delightful summer treats like patbingsu, the traditional shaved ice topped with red beans, or naengmyeon, the traditional cold noodle dish, are loved by both adults and kids.

Now I'd like to describe what winter is like in Korea. From early December, the temperature usually starts to drop noticeably and it gets freezing cold until March. Gangwon-do in particular is famous for its heavy snow, thanks to the Taebaek mountain range, the longest and highest range in Korea. Along its slopes, you'll find plenty of resorts where people enjoy skiing, sledding, you name it, so tons of people flock there every winter to make the most of it.

All in all, though I do miss the gentle days of spring and fall, I've come to appreciate the extremes of summer and winter also, from cooling off at the beach to carving down a snowy slope. That's it, Eva

children.script:
Wow Eva, that reminds me of my terrible memory. I did have a shivering experience that happened to me at Jeju airport last summer.

As I mentioned earlier, tons of people flock to Jeju island in summer, and my family and I also went there for our summer vacation last year. It was a three-day trip and the weather while we were there was picture-perfect. But here's the thing, Jeju is notorious for its strong winds, and many typhoons tend to strike the island in summer. And wouldn't you know it, on the exact day we were supposed to fly back from Jeju to Incheon, the wind suddenly picked up, out of nowhere. Bursts of lightning lit up the sky, and the sound of strong winds was very loud.

In the end, our flight was delayed for five hours, and we had no choice but to wait at the airport. We managed to kill some time in the airline lounge, but my kids were bored out of their minds, crying and throwing tantrums the whole time. By the time we finally boarded, I was completely drained.

After going through that incident, I try to avoid traveling to Jeju in summer. It's also too hot anyway, so I'd rather go in spring or fall. Eva, have you ever run into a similar travel headache?

As you know, the Shilla is by far the most famous, traditional, and historic hotel in Korea. It has many facilities in it, there are restaurants, bars, and even an arcade where you can shop for luxury collections!

The moment I arrived at the lobby, the staff took care of the valet parking for me. They pulled our heavy luggage right out of the trunk and carried it up to our room safely. The staff who greeted us at check-in were incredibly professional and warm, I was blown away. Once we got to the room, there was a welcome amenity waiting for us, along with a handwritten greeting letter. How thoughtful they were!

The room itself was spacious and clean, and since we stayed on the 27th floor, we had the privilege of a spectacular view of Namsan right from our window. But my favorite part of the room was, without a doubt, the bed. The bedding was flawless, and the plush texture of the quilt was so unforgettable that I ended up buying the same one for my house. Even though I spent my fortune, it was worth every penny.

Ah, that reminds me of how badly I need a vacation! Eva, do you enjoy traveling too?

Oh Eva, that's a great question, because I've noticed this shift happening in my country these days.

Compared to the past, way more restaurants nowadays are offering healthy options like low-calorie food and vegan dishes. I've actually heard that with the rise of obesity treatment drugs, some people say fewer people feel the need to diet these days. But honestly, I don't think that's slowing down the trend toward healthy food at all. From vegan menus to acai berry smoothies, many health-food chains are popping up everywhere in Korea.

This actually reminds me of a personal experience. Years ago, when I visited Hawaii, I tried tuna poke for the first time, and I was completely blown away. Not only was the dish delicious, but it was also surprisingly low in calories. I ended up eating poke almost every single day for the rest of that trip! You know what? There's a poke place near my office that serves something pretty close to that I had in Hawaii, so often I stop by there whenever I'm craving that same flavor.

Overall, I think this shift toward healthier menus is a great trend. How's your appetite, Eva?

children.name: food contamination incident
children.full: Food can get contaminated because of bacteria. It can go bad or become toxic. Tell me about an incident you heard on the news regarding this issue. What was the problem? How was it dealt with?
children.script:
Wow Eva, that's such a tough question, so let me think about it for a second. Well, one case that comes to mind is a mass food poisoning outbreak at a famous seafood restaurant that I saw on the news.

At first, everyone just assumed it happened because of the hot, humid summer weather. But after some investigation, it turned out the restaurant had been completely careless about hygiene, leaving ingredients exposed to the heat blast for a long time. It was shocking to see such a contrast between the elegant, upscale dining area and the filthy, unhygienic kitchen.

You know what? Actually I had a similar thing that happened before. On a trip to Busan, I had some oysters at a seafood restaurant, and not long after, I came down with norovirus. It was brutal, I was throwing up for three straight days and couldn't keep a single thing down, not even water. I remember lying in bed feeling completely drained, and I couldn't step out of the bed.

All in all, both that news story and my own experience taught me the same lesson. Never try seafood in summer! Eva, be careful when you visit Korea in summer!
